label: AI tip of the day
items: Ask a chatbot to list its assumptions, then check the two that matter most.
Paste only what you would be happy to see on a postcard: chatbots are not private diaries.
A model that sounds sure is not the same as a model that is right. Verify names, dates and numbers.
Give the AI a role, a goal, a format and an example. Four short lines beat one long paragraph.
If an answer feels too perfect, ask: "What would a sceptic say about this?"
Ask for sources, then open them. If the link does not exist, the claim may not either.
Hearing a loved one in distress on the phone? Hang up and call back on their usual number. Voices can be cloned.
Turn on two-factor authentication for your AI accounts: your chat history is valuable to attackers.
Break big tasks into steps: outline first, then each section, then a final edit.
Reverse-image search a shocking photo before sharing. Fake images spread fastest.
Use AI to explain a hard idea "like I am 12", then ask it to quiz you to check you understood.
Benchmarks are tests, not guarantees. Ask how a model does on tasks like yours.
Check the privacy settings of every AI tool you use: training on your data is often a toggle.
Prompt injection: text hidden in a web page can try to steer an AI assistant. Be careful letting assistants act on untrusted content.
When translating, ask for the literal and the natural version side by side.
Ask AI to proofread rather than rewrite when you want to keep your own voice.
Open-weight models can run on your own computer so your text never leaves it.
A "hallucination" is a confident invention. They are more common on obscure facts and recent events.
Always keep a human in charge of decisions about health, money, law or safety.
Use AI to brainstorm 20 ideas, then pick three and develop them yourself.
Tokens are small chunks of text; longer prompts and replies cost more and can hit limits.
Save prompts that work in a note so you can reuse them.
Be polite and specific. Clear instructions give clearer results than clever tricks.
Treat AI-generated code like code from a stranger: read it, test it, and never paste secrets into it.
Notice the incentives behind AI headlines: launches, funding and fears all have a promotional side.
Ask the model to say "I do not know" when it is unsure; many assistants follow that instruction.
Synthetic voices and faces are getting good. Agree a family safe word for emergencies.
For research, ask AI for keywords and questions to search, then read primary sources yourself.
Change one thing at a time when improving a prompt, so you know what helped.
Learning the vocabulary (token, context window, RAG) makes AI news far easier to follow.
